```{r} 
#| echo: FALSE
#| output: FALSE
#| message: FALSE

library(janitor)
install.packages("tinytable")
library(tinytable)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(naniar)
library(tidyr)
library(kable)

```

The goal of this report is to preform the preliminary data analysis in preparation for the panel regression we will be conducting. We are examining the association between armed conflict and several mortality outcomes. 

EXPOSURE = Armed Conflict (Binary -- Y(1), N(0))
OUTCOME(S) = Rates per 100,000 live births (Continuous) 
1. Maternal Mortality 
2. Neonatal Mortality 
3. Infant Mortality 
4. Under 5 Mortality 

We will begin by examining the variable types, names, and summary statistics. 

```{r} 
#| echo: TRUE

raw_data <- read.csv("data/processed/Merged_Data.csv", header=TRUE) |>
    clean_names()

head(raw_data)
```

```{r}
tail(raw_data)
```

```{r}
slice_sample(raw_data, n=6)
```

Now we can look at the variable types

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| output: TRUE
glimpse(raw_data)
```


We see that the mortality variables are dbl = numeric with decimal places. We see amed conflict is an integer. 

Total conflicts is also an integer, same with OECD, and year. 

The rest of the covariates are dbl --> which algin. 

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
summary(raw_data)
```

We can summize the following:
- Year is between 2009 to 2019 
- Maternal mortality has a very high max (2480 deaths per 100 000)
- There are NAs for infant under 5, and neonatal (20) 
- There are 426 NAs for maternal mortality 
- armed conflict has no NA values 
- There appears to be no 'abnormal' negative values for the covariates and such 

#quick check for duplicated rows#

```{r}
sum(duplicated(raw_data))
```

There are none, so we are good to go! 

**##Distribution of Outcomes**
We can create a histogram for this (for each mortality variable)

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE 
#| output: TRUE

ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = maternal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

- We can see its very right skewed
- Very few "high" observations making it difficult to see majority of the observation values that lie in the lower range
- We can use log transform to look at **relative differences**. Shrink the scale to make it easier to examine.

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| output: TRUE 
ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = maternal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_x_log10()

```

Clearly we can see that mortality rates are very right skewed as most concentrate in the lower value range. small number of observations at very high rates. 


```{r}
ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = neonatal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()

ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = neonatal_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_x_log10()
```

Here we can see a lot of neonatal mortality is on the slightly higher end value wise. 

```{r}
ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = infant_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()

ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = infant_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_x_log10()
```

Similar to neonatal mortality
```{r}
ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = under5_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()

ggplot(raw_data, aes(x = under5_mortality)) +
  geom_histogram()+
  scale_x_log10()
```

Clearly we see maternal mortality is much lower compared to younger-onset mortality (infant, neonatal, under5)

**##Examine maternal mortality**

```{r}
summary(raw_data$maternal_mortality)

#lets examine the max observation 

raw_data %>%
  filter(maternal_mortality == max(maternal_mortality, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Based on that observation -> SLE (Sierra Leonne), had 4493 conflicts 
Let's confirm with the raw data. Seems to be the case. very consistently high across all years. This is why the data is super skewed. 

Some background research --> Sierra Leonne civil war that occured during that time. 

**##EXAMINE FREQUENCY OF OUTCOME WITHIN EACH##**
Now we will explore the proportion of 'armed_conflict' overall 

First we convert to a factor variable rather than numerical 

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| output: FALSE
conflict_data <- raw_data |> mutate(armed_conflict=as.factor(armed_conflict)) 
summary(conflict_data$armed_conflict) #for counts 
prop.table(table(conflict_data$armed_conflict)) #for proportions 
```

81 % of countries across all years did not experience an armed conflict
18.9% experienced an armed conflict 
This is overall so we can get the prop by year 

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| output: TRUE

yearly <- conflict_data %>% group_by(year) %>% 
    summarize(percent_conflict = 100*mean(armed_conflict==1, na.rm=TRUE))
#na.rm = true just means include na observations (there aren't any i believe)


ggplot(yearly, aes(x = year, y = percent_conflict)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") #identity to make bar height reflect the percentages in y.Can also use geom_col()

```

**##MISSING DATA**

Now we need to examine the missingness within each variable. We will pay particular close attention to our exposure and outcomes of interest. 

```{r}
pct_miss_case(conflict_data)
```

85% of cases have some sort of missing value 


```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| output: TRUE
gg_miss_var(conflict_data, show_pct=TRUE)
```

Clearly we can see:
- Earthquake and drought have high missingness counts
- our exposure (armed conflict) seems to have no missing data (yay)
- Some outcomes have missing data (maternal_mortalityu, under5, neonatal, infant)

Lets quantify the exact amount however for the exposure and outcomes. 

```{r}
missing_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(conflict_data),
  Missing_n = colSums(is.na(conflict_data)),
  Missing_pct = round(colMeans(is.na(conflict_data)) * 100, 1))

#format it in a nice table 
kable(
  missing_table,
  col.names = c("Variable", "Missing (n)", "Missing (%)"),
  caption = "Missingness quanitified by variable"
)
```


We should explore the earthquake and drought, by exposure and outcome to determine the reason for missingness (MNAR, MAR, MCAR) 


```{r}
#| error: FALSE
#| output: TRUE 
gg_miss_upset(conflict_data)
```

This upset plot helps us see whether variables tend to be missing together. Earthquake and drought seem to be. 
Set size = number of missing observations. Interaction size is how many they have in common. 

This plot seems to suggest that earthquake and drought are missing together, which may indicate we should explore why. 

This is likely actually due to the way we had coded the earthquake and drought variables. Since when we merged all the final data sets, any countries that had no earthquake or drought, were just coded as NA. 


```{r}
conflict_data_recode <- conflict_data %>%
  mutate(
    earthquake = replace_na(earthquake, 0),
    drought = replace_na(drought, 0)
  )
gg_miss_upset(conflict_data_recode)

```

Now for maternal mortality, let's try to explore the reasons for missingness. Seem to potentially not have that data available. Lets look at these observations closely: 


```{r}
conflict_data_recode %>%
  filter(is.na(maternal_mortality)) %>%
  count(iso, sort = TRUE)
```

So this tells us countries with AND, DMA, and MHL iso codes have 20 missing values. 
DMA = Dominica
MHL = Marshall Islands
AND = Andorra


```{r}
conflict_data_recode %>%
  filter(is.na(maternal_mortality)) %>%
  count(year, sort = TRUE)
```

Majority in 2018 and 2019. 

Overall we can say:
*Missing maternal mortality data were concentrated in specific countries (Andorra, Dominica, and Marshall Islands) and primarily occurred in 2018 and 2019. Because the missingness appears related to observed characteristics of the data (country and year), it is unlikely to be Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) and is more consistent with a Missing At Random (MAR). We will likely retain these covariates regardless.*

**##Dealing with Missing Data!**

We will use a complete case analysis approach to remove observations that are missing any of the outcomes and exposures. 

```{r}
conflict_data_1 <- conflict_data %>% 
  drop_na(c(maternal_mortality, neonatal_mortality, infant_mortality, under5_mortality))


nrow(conflict_data_1)
```

Therefore we can see a total of 444 observations were removed. We will likely use sensitivity analyses later on to check this decision. 

##Understanding relationships between variables## 

```{r}
#| echo: TRUE
#| output: TRUE 
conflict_data_1 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = armed_conflict, y = maternal_mortality, alpha = 0.1)) +
  geom_boxplot()

conflict_data_1 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = armed_conflict, y = maternal_mortality, alpha = 0.1)) +
  geom_violin()+
  geom_boxplot(width=0.1)

```

We do see the median maternal mortality is lower among no armed conflict, compared to armed conflict. Suggest country years with armed conflict have higher mortatlity (maternal)

Conflict group has a greater spread (values extend high). Seem to be very skewed (most groups are on the lowe rend but there is a tail on the higher end)

Similar trends for neonatal in terms of median in armed 0 vs 1. However much more higher values, not as skewed.
